client: I got a rejection letter from my dream university last week, and honestly it's been hitting me harder than I expected. I keep thinking about all the work I put into that application and wondering if I just wasn't good enough, like maybe I never was. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds genuinely painful — there's a quiet heaviness in how you're sharing this, like you're holding a lot beneath the surface even as the words come quickly. That thought, "maybe I was never good enough," is one worth gently examining together, because a rejection letter reflects one decision by one committee on one day, not the full measure of who you are or what you're capable of. I'm really glad you gave this a shot, and I think there's meaningful work we can do here together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it's hard not to feel like you're just... supposed to say that, you know? Like, that's the therapist response. The thing is, this wasn't my first rejection — it's the third program in two years, and at some point doesn't the pattern start to mean something?
therapist: That skepticism you're bringing is actually really valuable here — you're not looking for empty reassurance, you want something real, and that matters. You're right that patterns can carry meaning, but the question worth sitting with is: what story are you telling yourself *about* that pattern — is it "I'm learning and this path is harder than expected," or has it become "this is proof I'm fundamentally not enough"? There's something in the way you're speaking — like you're working hard to stay measured while carrying something that feels quite heavy — that tells me this third rejection has landed somewhere deeper than just disappointment.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, you're right that it landed somewhere deeper — I think I've been trying to dress it up as just "career frustration" because that feels more manageable than admitting how much it's shaken my sense of who I am. The "not enough" story... I don't know, it's not like I consciously chose it, it just kind of crept in after the second rejection and now it feels almost factual, not like a story at all. That's what scares me — I can't tell anymore where the evidence ends and the catastrophizing begins.
therapist: The fact that you can name exactly that — "I can't tell where the evidence ends and the catastrophizing begins" — is actually a really important moment of clarity, even if it doesn't feel like one right now. There's something in how you're speaking, soft and quick, like you're trying to get these words out before doubt catches up with you, that tells me this took courage to admit. That blurring between fact and story is precisely where CBT can help — because when a belief has been repeated enough times in painful moments, it *feels* like bedrock truth, and part of our work together is gently testing whether it actually holds up under scrutiny.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that distinction is possible — like, that I could actually separate what's real from what my brain is just... spinning out. But honestly, when I'm in the middle of it, when it's 2am and I'm convinced everyone at work thinks I'm incompetent, it doesn't feel like a story at all, it feels like the most obvious truth in the world. I guess I'm just not sure how you "test" something that feels that certain.
therapist: That 2am feeling you're describing — where the thought feels less like a thought and more like gravity — is one of the most disorienting parts of what you're going through, and I can hear in your voice right now a kind of urgent searching, like you're genuinely trying to find a foothold. The way we start to test something that certain isn't by arguing with it head-on, but by asking one small question: "What would I need to see to know this *wasn't* true?" — because if no evidence could ever change the belief, that's actually a clue that we're dealing with a story, not a fact. You don't have to believe that yet, but I wonder if there's even one moment at work recently that doesn't quite fit the "everyone thinks I'm incompetent" narrative.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, but honestly, my first instinct is that any moment I could come up with would just be an exception, you know? Like my brain would immediately say "okay but that one time doesn't count because they were just being polite" or "that was a fluke." I guess there was this one meeting last week where my manager actually used my idea without changing it, but even as I say that out loud, part of me is already explaining it away.
therapist: Notice what just happened — you brought forward real evidence, and then watched your mind immediately move to discredit it, almost before you'd finished the sentence, and there's something in how quickly and intensely you're speaking right now that tells me that dismissal reflex is very fast and very automatic. That pattern *is* the thing worth examining — not whether your manager's response "counts," but why your mind has a ready-made reason to disqualify anything that contradicts the story. What would it mean for you if that moment in the meeting actually *did* count?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I guess... if it actually counted, it would mean I'm not as invisible at work as I feel like I am, and that's kind of terrifying to sit with. Because if people do notice me and I'm still this anxious and lonely, then I can't just blame it on being overlooked anymore. I don't know what to do with that.
therapist: What you just said takes real courage to sit with — there's something in your voice right now, soft and a little unsteady, like you've just touched something you've been carefully avoiding, and that makes complete sense. You've just identified something really important: that the loneliness and anxiety might not be *caused* by being overlooked, but might have a life of their own that needs its own attention. That's not a dead end — that's actually the beginning of understanding what's really going on beneath the surface.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess that makes sense, but it also kind of scares me a little, if I'm being honest. Like, if the loneliness isn't just about other people not noticing me, then it's something I'm carrying around inside myself, and that feels way harder to fix. I don't even know where you'd start with something like that.
therapist: The fear in what you're sharing is real, and there's something in your voice — a kind of quiet tension, like you're bracing yourself — that tells me this realization feels heavy right now. But I want to gently offer a different frame: the fact that you're carrying this *inside* you actually means it's something you have more access to and more influence over than other people's perceptions ever were. We don't have to know where it ends to know where to start — and you've already started, right here, by naming it honestly.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that, I really do. But it's hard not to feel like "having access to it" just means I'm stuck alone with it, you know? Like, it's not exactly comforting to know the problem lives inside me when I don't even fully trust my own mind right now.
therapist: That sense of being "stuck alone with it" — especially when you don't fully trust your own thinking right now — is one of the loneliest feelings there is, and I can hear something in your voice, a kind of stretched tension, like you're holding yourself together carefully while saying something that really costs you. But I want to gently push back on one thing: you are not alone with it right now, in this moment, and learning to trust your mind again isn't something you have to figure out by yourself before we can move forward — that rebuilding of trust is actually something we do together, gradually, one small moment of evidence at a time.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but there's this other part that keeps thinking... even if I'm not alone right now, in this room, I still have to go home tonight and sit with all of it by myself. And honestly, I'm not sure building trust "one small moment at a time" is going to feel like enough when the anxiety just kind of swallows everything whole and I can't even tell what's real anymore.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, pitched high, like the words are trying to outrun something — tells me this fear of tonight, of being alone with it, is very present and very real in this moment, not just a hypothetical. That feeling of anxiety "swallowing everything whole" is something I want to take seriously, and I'd like to ask you directly: when you're in those moments alone at night, are you safe? Because before we talk about building trust slowly, I want to make sure we're also thinking about what support looks like for you in those hardest moments.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I'm safe, I'm not going to do anything to hurt myself, it's not like that. It's more like... I just sit there and the anxiety kind of takes over and I can't turn my brain off, and I end up going over everything I've done wrong that day, every awkward thing I said, every way I probably let someone down. It's exhausting but it's not dangerous, I just hate how alone it feels when there's no one to even text at midnight who would actually get it.
therapist: Thank you for telling me that clearly — and I hear you, that exhausting loop of replaying every misstep, every awkward moment, alone at midnight with no one to reach out to, is its own kind of pain that deserves to be taken seriously. There's something in your voice right now — soft, almost tired, like you've been carrying this particular weight for a long time — that tells me this nightly ritual of self-review has become one of the heaviest parts of your day. That pattern of mentally "going over everything you did wrong" is actually something we can work with directly — it has a name, it's called rumination, and there are real, concrete tools that can help interrupt it before it swallows the whole night.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
